title: Denmark Ferries Its Jews to Sweden
text:
Germany occupied Denmark in 1940 but for years left much of its government in place, and the country's roughly 7,500 Jews were not deported. In late September 1943 that changed: Berlin ordered a roundup for the night of 1 to 2 October.

Georg Duckwitz, a German diplomat in Copenhagen, leaked the plan to Danish Social Democrat leaders. The warning spread fast. On 29 September, the eve of the Jewish New Year, Rabbi Marcus Melchior told his congregation to leave their homes and hide. Over the following days, ordinary Danes took Jewish neighbors and strangers into their apartments, summer houses, churches and hospitals. Doctors admitted people under false names. Students, policemen and resistance members guided them toward the coast.

From fishing villages along the Oresund, fishermen carried them across the narrow strait to neutral Sweden, mostly at night, hidden in holds and under nets. Sweden publicly announced it would take them in. Some fishermen charged high fares, especially at first, and others took people for little or nothing. Within about three weeks, some 7,000 Jews and several hundred non-Jewish relatives had reached Sweden.

The German raids caught fewer than 500, who were sent to the Theresienstadt camp. Danish officials kept pressing for their welfare, and most of them survived the war. Altogether, more than nine in ten of Denmark's Jews were saved.
lesson: When many ordinary people act quickly and together, even a powerful threat can be defeated. Collective courage spreads when the first few act.
people: Georg Duckwitz, Rabbi Marcus Melchior, Danish citizens and fishermen
location: Copenhagen and the Oresund coast, Denmark, and Sweden
source: Bo Lidegaard, Countrymen (2013); Yad Vashem, The Rescue of Danish Jewry
